newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl says Germany will meet 3.0 pct EMU target.
newsitem.headline: Kohl says Germany will meet 3.0 pct EMU target.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl, going on the offensive against his critics, said on Tuesday Germany would meet the 3.0 percent deficit-to-GDP target for Europe's single currency and its 1999 deadline.

Kohl, at a Munich business conference attended by leading Euro-sceptic and Bavarian state premier Edmund Stoiber, said the German parliament had given its word it would only agree to the euro if the criteria were met.
Delaying the project, as Stoiber has been demanding now that economists doubt countries like Germany and France can meet the strict deficit target, would be wrong, he added.

Kohl said Germany expected 2.5 percent economic growth in 1997 and three percent in 1998, enabling it to meet the deficit criteria in both years. Dramatic gaps in Bonn's budget have led to charges Bonn would not make the grade.
"We're staying with 3.0 -- that's no problem -- and with the schedule," Kohl told about 1,500 Bavarian employers on the 50th anniversary of their association.
Kohl has until now avoided taking the hardline position that the three percent target mentioned in the Maastricht treaty had to be interpreted as 3.0 percent and not higher.
But a mounting campaign by Stoiber, who fears the far-right could exploit the issue at next year's Bavarian state election, apparently prompted him to change.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, chairman of Bavaria's ruling Christian Social Union (CSU) and a bitter rival of Stoiber, has long demanded a strict interpretation.
In his speech, Kohl recalled that parliament had demanded a strict interpretation of the convergence criteria when it approved the 1991 Maastricht treaty.
"That stands, it is binding, there is no use discussing it any more," he declared.

Stoiber, who has made increasingly vociferous calls to delay the euro if the criteria are not met exactly, said the anniversary meeting in Munich's Philharmonic Hall was not the place to continue the Euro-fight and thanked Kohl for his clear statement on EMU.
But he added: "The sustainable and strict application of the convergence criteria play a central role... There will be a lot more discussion about this."
Kohl avoided mentioning Stoiber's Euro-sceptical stand but looked beyond the premier sitting in the front row to urge the business leaders to reject his arguments.
"Whoever says we can't make the criteria is wrong," he said. "That will not be the government's position."
He also stressed that Germany had won a stability pact and an independent central bank to ensure the new currency would be as stable as the deutsche mark.

The mark was a piece of Germany's post-war identity, a symbol older than the Federal Republic itself, and Bonn would only give it up if it had firm guarantees its replacement would be stable, he said.
"If we Gemans make this contribution to Europe, then we have good reason to say it has to be a stable currency."
